title: Ash on the windshield
note: Fictional unit and patients. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: You are the charge nurse of a 12-station unit in Tanauan, Batangas. Fine gray ash covers the roads and cars after an eruption. The first shift starts at 6:00 a.m. The waiting-area windows are open, and the water room draws from a rooftop tank with a loose cover.

n1.prompt: What do you do before the first patient arrives?

choices.text: Close up, set an ash-cleaning point, cover the intakes and tank, masks ready.
choices.feedback: Close, cover, clean: keep ash out of the building, the air and the water. Close windows and doors; ask the building staff to cover the air intakes and secure the rooftop tank cover.

choices.text: Start the first patients on time, then close the windows and doors once everyone is connected.
choices.feedback: Every minute with open windows lets ash in.
choices.then: You close up after the first connections.

choices.text: Keep the windows open for ventilation, as usual, since the unit gets warm without them.
choices.feedback: Ash irritates eyes and lungs and gets into equipment.
choices.then: Ash drifts across the waiting area; you close the windows.

n2.scene: At 6:20 a.m. the water technician reports the pre-filter pressure drop is rising fast.

choices.text: Stop new starts; the technician checks and tests the water; follow the water failure steps.
choices.feedback: Ash may be entering the water. No new patient starts on water that may fail. Check the tank and filters, and keep to the steps until the water is released.

choices.text: Ask the technician to bypass the pre-filter so the pressure holds and the sessions can go on.
choices.feedback: Bypassing a filter lets ash and particles further into the treatment train, putting every patient on the loop at risk.
choices.then: The technician refuses and stops new starts until the water is tested.

n3.scene: Water tests pass and are signed at 8:00 a.m. An older patient with chronic lung disease arrives coughing after waiting outside in the ash.
n3.prompt: What happens before he is connected?

choices.text: The physician-on-duty examines him first; he wears a mask.
choices.feedback: A clinical assessment comes before connection. Breathing and oxygen saturation; call the attending nephrologist if he is unwell.

choices.text: Connect him as usual; the cough will settle once he is indoors and away from the ash.
choices.feedback: He may need hospital care, not a routine session.
choices.then: Twenty minutes in he is breathless; the physician-on-duty examines him then.

end.title: Mid-morning
end.text: The building is closed against ash, the water was tested and released before treatments resumed, and the coughing patient was examined first. Two staff who could not travel safely stayed home.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Close, cover, clean: the building, the intakes, and people at the door.
  • Ash in the water is a water event; never bypass a filter to keep pressure up.
  • Patients exposed to ash or heat are examined before connection when they are unwell.
